questions.q: A 35-year-old man from rural Bihar presents with a well-defined hypopigmented patch on his left forearm. There is loss of sensation to light touch over the patch, and the left ulnar nerve is thickened and tender. Slit-skin smear is negative. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: BT leprosy presents with a small number of hypopigmented, well-defined patches with peripheral nerve involvement. Nerve thickening and tenderness are prominent features. TT has only 1 patch with no nerve involvement (or minimal). Negative SSS confirms paucibacillary spectrum.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman on multidrug therapy for lepromatous leprosy develops sudden onset of painful erythematous nodules over the face, trunk, and extremities, accompanied by fever and arthritis. The phenomenon responsible is:
questions.exp: ENL (Type 2 reaction) occurs in BL and LL leprosy and is mediated by immune complex deposition (Type III hypersensitivity). It presents with painful erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic features. It is treated with thalidomide or steroids.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with circular scaly patches on the scalp with broken hair stubs. KOH preparation shows endothrix pattern of infection. The causative organism is MOST likely:
questions.exp: Trichophyton violaceum and T. tonsurans cause endothrix tinea capitis (spores fill the hair shaft). T. violaceum is the most common cause of endothrix tinea capitis in India. Microsporum species cause ectothrix infection. Epidermophyton floccosum does not infect hair.

questions.q: A 45-year-old immunocompetent farmer presents with a slowly enlarging, painless verrucous plaque on the dorsum of his right foot. Histopathology shows 'Medlar bodies' (sclerotic bodies). The treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: The description is classic for chromoblastomycosis. Medlar bodies (brown, thick-walled sclerotic cells with cross-septation) are pathognomonic. Treatment of choice is itraconazole 200 mg/day or terbinafine 500 mg/day; combination therapy is preferred for extensive disease.

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy presents with honey-crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in chains. The MOST feared complication of this condition in India is:
questions.exp: Honey-crusted perioral/perinasal lesions with Gram-positive cocci in chains point to impetigo caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. Post-streptococcal acute glomerulonephritis is the main nephritogenic complication of cutaneous streptococcal infection (unlike throat infection, which causes rheumatic fever). Rheumatic fever does not follow skin streptococcal infection.

questions.q: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with rapidly spreading gangrenous infection of the scrotum and perineum with crepitus on palpation. Blood culture grows mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms. The MOST appropriate initial management is:
opts: Urgent surgical debridement plus IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
questions.exp: This is Fournier's gangrene (necrotizing fasciitis of perineum). Immediate surgical debridement is the cornerstone of treatment; antibiotics alone are ineffective. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobes) are started concurrently. Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 count 80 cells/µL) presents with profuse vegetating, hyperkeratotic crusted lesions all over his body. Scrapings show numerous mites at all stages. The condition is:
questions.exp: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies occurs in immunocompromised patients (HIV, steroid use, elderly). It features widespread hyperkeratotic plaques teeming with thousands of mites, making it highly contagious. Treatment requires oral ivermectin plus topical scabicide.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated, clean-based genital ulcer with a non-tender inguinal lymph node (bilateral). VDRL is negative. Darkfield microscopy of the serous exudate from the base of the ulcer would show:
questions.exp: A painless, indurated, clean-based genital ulcer (chancre) with non-tender bilateral lymphadenopathy is primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Darkfield microscopy of serous exudate shows corkscrew-shaped, motile treponemes. VDRL may be negative early in primary syphilis.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with clusters of tender vesicles on the vulva and perianal skin following a flu-like illness. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. The drug of choice for suppressive therapy to reduce recurrences is:
questions.exp: Genital herpes (HSV-2) suppressive therapy uses acyclovir 400 mg twice daily (or valacyclovir 500 mg once daily, famciclovir 250 mg twice daily). Suppressive therapy reduces frequency of recurrences by 70-80% and decreases transmission risk.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with soft, fleshy, cauliflower-like growths on the perianal skin. PCR reveals HPV type 6. The treatment with the highest recurrence rate is:
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata (genital warts) caused by HPV 6 and 11. Podophyllin is a provider-applied cytotoxic agent with high recurrence rates (up to 65%) and significant side effects. Patient-applied imiquimod and cryotherapy have lower recurrence rates. Surgical excision has the lowest recurrence rate.

questions.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with tense blisters arising on normal-looking skin over the trunk and flexural areas. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone. The target antigen is:
questions.exp: Tense blisters on normal skin in an elderly patient with linear IgG/C3 at BMZ on DIF is classic for bullous pemphigoid. Target antigens are BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230, both components of hemidesmosomal complexes. Desmoglein 1 and 3 are targets in pemphigus; type VII collagen is the target in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with painful erosions in the mouth for 3 months followed by flaccid blisters on the trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive. Histology shows suprabasal acantholysis. ELISA detects antibodies against desmoglein 3 and desmoglein 1. The MOST appropriate treatment is:
questions.exp: Mucocutaneous pemphigus vulgaris (anti-Dsg3 and anti-Dsg1 antibodies) requires immunosuppression. High-dose oral corticosteroids remain the mainstay; rituximab (anti-CD20) is now the preferred adjuvant steroid-sparing agent with superior remission rates. Dapsone is used in IgA pemphigus and linear IgA disease.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with photosensitive butterfly-shaped erythema over the face, oral ulcers, and arthritis. ANA titre is 1:640 (homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA antibody is positive. Renal biopsy shows diffuse proliferative changes. WHO/ISN class of nephritis and the recommended treatment are:
opts: Class IV nephritis; high-dose steroids plus mycophenolate mofetil
questions.exp: Diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis is ISN/RPS Class IV — the most severe form requiring aggressive immunosuppression. Standard induction therapy is high-dose corticosteroids plus mycophenolate mofetil (or cyclophosphamide). Hydroxychloroquine is used as background therapy in all SLE patients.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, dysphagia, skin tightening over the fingers and face, and teleangiectasias. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. This pattern is associated with:
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody is the hallmark of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). Diffuse SSc is associated with anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70). Risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension is higher in limited SSc.

questions.q: A 6-year-old girl develops a photodistributed violaceous rash over the eyelids (heliotrope), Gottron papules over the knuckles, and proximal muscle weakness. CK is markedly elevated. What is the MOST important malignancy screening consideration in this patient?
opts: Age-appropriate screening only, as childhood dermatomyositis is rarely paraneoplastic
Immediate CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and tumour markers
questions.exp: In juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM), malignancy is rare (unlike adult dermatomyositis where 15-30% is paraneoplastic). JDM is primarily an autoimmune vasculopathy. Age-appropriate standard care without extensive malignancy workup is appropriate. In adults, a thorough malignancy screen is mandatory.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with well-defined, erythematous, silvery-scaled plaques over the elbows, knees, and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. Histopathology shows parakeratosis, elongated rete ridges, Munro micro-abscesses, and reduced granular layer. The primary event in the pathogenesis is:
opts: Keratinocyte hyperproliferation driven by Th1 and Th17 cytokines (IL-17, TNF-α, IL-23)
questions.exp: Psoriasis is driven by Th1/Th17 lymphocytes. Key cytokines include IL-23 (produced by dendritic cells, driving Th17 differentiation), IL-17A, IL-17F, and TNF-α. These cause keratinocyte hyperproliferation (transit time reduced from 28 to 3-4 days). This understanding drives biologic therapy targets.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with plaque psoriasis on biologics develops arthritis mutilans with 'pencil-in-cup' deformity on X-ray. The biologic agent that is FDA-approved BOTH for psoriasis AND psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and specifically targets IL-17A is:
questions.exp: Secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) and ixekizumab (anti-IL-17A) are both approved for plaque psoriasis and PsA. The question specifies IL-17A target — both qualify. However, secukinumab was first-in-class; for the purpose of this question, secukinumab is the landmark IL-17A inhibitor approved for PsA. Ustekinumab targets IL-12/23 (p40 subunit). Guselkumab targets IL-23 (p19).

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman on carbamazepine for epilepsy develops fever, painful erosions of the mouth and conjunctivae, and extensive skin detachment involving >30% BSA with a positive Nikolsky sign. Skin biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis with subepidermal split. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: TEN is defined as drug-induced full-thickness epidermal necrosis with mucosal involvement and >30% BSA detachment. SJS involves <10% BSA; SJS-TEN overlap is 10-30%. Carbamazepine is a high-risk drug. SSSS shows subcorneal split (superficial) on biopsy and is caused by S. aureus toxins.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man on allopurinol develops fever, diffuse morbilliform exanthem, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, and internal organ involvement (hepatitis, pneumonitis). Eosinophilia is present. The syndrome is:
opts: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)
questions.exp: DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) presents 2-8 weeks after drug initiation with fever, morbilliform rash, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and internal organ involvement. High-risk drugs include allopurinol, antiepileptics, and sulfonamides. HHV-6 reactivation is implicated in pathogenesis.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a pearly papule with rolled telangiectatic borders and central ulceration on his nose. Sun exposure history is significant. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels. The MOST common type of this tumour and the recommended treatment is:
questions.exp: Pearly nodule with rolled borders, telangiectasia, and central ulceration on the nose is nodular basal cell carcinoma (most common type, 60-80%). Mohs micrographic surgery is the treatment of choice for high-risk/head-and-neck BCC due to the highest cure rates and maximal tissue conservation.

questions.q: A 55-year-old fair-skinned man presents with an asymmetric pigmented lesion on the back, with irregular borders and multiple shades of brown, black, and red. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is positive. The MOST important histopathological prognostic factor for melanoma is:
questions.exp: Breslow thickness (measured in mm from the granular layer to the deepest tumour cell) is the single most important prognostic factor for primary melanoma. It determines staging, surgical margins, and the indication for sentinel node biopsy (>0.8 mm or any thickness with ulceration).

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman with longstanding lymphedema of the right arm after mastectomy develops multiple violaceous nodules and plaques. Biopsy shows anastomosing vascular channels with pleomorphic endothelial cells. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Stewart-Treves syndrome is lymphangiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema (classically post-mastectomy lymphedema). It is a high-grade vascular sarcoma with poor prognosis. Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and HIV/immunosuppression, not chronic lymphedema.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman undergoes a punch biopsy of a suspicious pigmented lesion. Post-procedure, she develops a hypertrophic, raised, pruritic scar that extends beyond the original wound boundary. The pathological basis is:
opts: Excessive fibroblast activity with collagen type I/III deposition extending beyond wound margins
Increased elastin deposition within wound limits
questions.exp: Keloids are caused by excessive fibroblast proliferation and collagen (predominantly type I and III) deposition that extends beyond the wound margins, unlike hypertrophic scars which remain within wound borders. Keloids have increased TGF-β signalling and decreased apoptosis of fibroblasts.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman is undergoing patch testing. After applying the allergen on Day 0, she is instructed to keep the patch in place for 48 hours. The patches are then read on Day 2 and Day 4. She develops a reaction at the nickel site only on Day 4 (negative on Day 2). This pattern indicates:
opts: Crescendo reaction (increasing from Day 2 to Day 4) — true allergic contact dermatitis
Decrescendo reaction — likely a false positive
questions.exp: True allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV hypersensitivity) often shows a crescendo pattern — absent or mild on Day 2 and increasing (or new) on Day 4. A reaction that appears only on Day 4 is a 'late' positive, still indicating sensitisation. A decrescendo reaction (stronger on Day 2, fading by Day 4) is more suggestive of irritant or false-positive reaction.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with discrete follicular papules and pustules predominantly on the face. Gram stain of the pustule content is negative. The lesion responds poorly to topical antibiotics but well to isotretinoin. The predominant pathogenic mechanism is:
opts: Comedone formation with Cutibacterium acnes triggering IL-1β and IL-17 mediated inflammation
questions.exp: Acne vulgaris pathogenesis involves: (1) sebaceous gland hypersecretion (androgen-driven), (2) follicular hyperkeratinisation forming microcomedones, (3) Cutibacterium acnes (formerly P. acnes) colonisation triggering TLR2-mediated IL-1β and IL-17 release, and (4) inflammation. Isotretinoin targets all four pathogenic factors.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman of Indian origin presents with bilateral, symmetrical hyperpigmentation over the cheeks, upper lip, and forehead that worsens with sun exposure. She is on oral contraceptive pills. Woods lamp examination shows enhancement of pigmentation. The MOST superficial layer involved is:
questions.exp: Melasma classification by Wood's lamp: epidermal type shows enhancement (accentuation) under Wood's lamp (365 nm UV) because the melanin in the epidermis absorbs UV. Dermal type shows no enhancement. Mixed type shows partial enhancement. Epidermal melasma responds best to depigmenting agents.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with depigmented macules over the face, hands, and knees. Wood's lamp shows chalky-white fluorescence. There is a family history of similar lesions. Skin biopsy shows complete absence of melanocytes. The management with the best evidence for repigmentation is:
questions.exp: Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB, 311 nm) is the gold standard treatment for widespread vitiligo. It stimulates residual follicular melanocyte reservoirs to migrate and repigment the skin. Topical tacrolimus is effective for localised/facial vitiligo. Hydroquinone depigments — it has no role in vitiligo repigmentation.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with palpable purpura over the lower limbs, haematuria, and RBC casts. Serum IgA is elevated and skin biopsy shows IgA deposits in vessel walls on DIF. The systemic disease is:
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is a small-vessel vasculitis characterised by IgA immune complex deposition. Classic tetrad: palpable purpura (lower limbs), arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement (IgA nephropathy). DIF shows IgA in vessel walls — this is pathognomonic. It is the most common vasculitis in children.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of intensely pruritic, erythematous, oedematous plaques that resolve within 24 hours without residual pigmentation. She reports that each lesion lasts less than 6 hours. The target of mast cell activation in this condition is:
opts: FcεRI on mast cells cross-linked by IgE bound to allergen
questions.exp: Urticaria results from mast cell degranulation triggered by IgE cross-linking on high-affinity IgE receptors (FcεRI) on mast cell surfaces. Released mediators (histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes) cause localised vasodilatation, increased permeability, and pruritus. Individual wheals resolve in <24 hours — this distinguishes urticaria from urticarial vasculitis.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy with a history of asthma and allergic rhinitis presents with flexural eczema on the antecubital and popliteal fossae since infancy. Serum IgE is markedly elevated. Filaggrin gene mutation is detected. The MOST direct consequence of loss-of-function filaggrin mutation on skin barrier is:
opts: Impaired cornification leading to increased transepidermal water loss (TEWL) and reduced skin surface acidity
questions.exp: Filaggrin (FLG) mutations cause impaired profilaggrin processing in the stratum corneum, reducing natural moisturising factor (NMF) production. This results in reduced skin barrier integrity, increased TEWL, elevated skin pH (reduced acidity), and enhanced allergen penetration — the primary defect in atopic dermatitis. It is the strongest single genetic risk factor for AD.
